scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for the parents to insist on knowing why their 17-year-old son is seeing a therapist. Let me start by understanding the situation better. The son has always been a normal, active, and social kid with many friends. Suddenly, he asks to see a therapist, which surprises his parents. They ask him why, but he doesn't want to share. Concerned, they send him to a therapist, and now he goes once a week. From the parents' perspective, he still seems the same, so they're trying to figure out what's going on. They consider possibilities like eating disorders or depression but don't see clear signs of those. They decide to ask the therapist for some insight, but the therapist refuses, citing confidentiality. The parents push further, asking at least for the reason, but the therapist still refuses. The next day, the son finds out they were trying to get information from the therapist and gets upset, insulting them and not talking to them the rest of the day. Now, the parents are questioning whether they were wrong to insist on knowing. They feel they deserve to know as his parents but are now dealing with the consequences of their actions. First, I need to consider the rights and responsibilities of both the parents and the therapist. Therapists are bound by confidentiality, which is crucial to building trust with their clients. Without confidentiality, clients, especially teenagers, might not feel safe to open up about their issues. On the other hand, parents have a right to know what's going on with their child, especially if they're paying for the therapy and are concerned about their well-being. But there's also the aspect of the son's privacy and autonomy. At 17, he's almost an adult, and he has the right to make decisions about his own mental health. Insisting on knowing the details of his therapy sessions could be seen as overstepping, especially if it leads to conflict and the son feeling betrayed or misunderstood. I also need to think about the potential consequences of the parents' actions. By pushing the therapist for information, they might have inadvertently caused their son to feel that his privacy is being invaded. This could lead to a breakdown in communication between the son and his parents, which is not ideal, especially if the son is going through a tough time and needs their support. Moreover, the parents' approach might have made the therapist feel uncomfortable or even in violation of their professional ethics. Therapists are trained to maintain boundaries, and parents insisting on information that's protected by confidentiality could strain the therapeutic relationship. On the other hand, the parents are coming from a place of concern and love. They want to support their son and understand what he's going through. It's natural for parents to worry and want to help, but they need to balance that with respecting their child's privacy and autonomy. Perhaps a better approach would have been for the parents to communicate their concerns to their son directly, expressing their worry and desire to support him without prying into the specifics of his therapy. They could have encouraged open dialogue, letting him know that they're there for him and that they respect his need for privacy. In summary, while the parents' intentions were good, their method of trying to get information from the therapist was likely overstepping and could have negative consequences. Respecting their son's privacy and focusing on open communication might have been a more effective approach.
